label: Claude Haiku 5.5
output:
# Four of Us on a Rota for Six

I should say at the outset that I am not a saint, and nobody who has seen me with a teapot would suggest otherwise. I am seventy-four, I was a bookkeeper for forty-one years, mostly for a builders' merchant in Dereham, and I spent a good part of my first year of retirement not quite knowing what to do with my Thursdays. I started volunteering at Wensum Vale in March 2022, and I am writing this because Bridget, our volunteer coordinator, has asked me to, and because we are two people short on the Thursday tea trolley in the day therapy unit.

The trolley runs from 1.30 to 4pm. We have four of us on a rota that is meant for six, since two left over the summer. One moved to Sheffield to be near her grandchildren, and the other had a knee operation and is not yet back on her feet. We are managing, but only just, and I would like us to stop managing.

The commitment is one Thursday a fortnight. That is it. Bridget runs the induction, which takes about two hours, and you also complete a short food hygiene course online, which the hospice pays for. You will not be asked to do anything clinical. You do not need any nursing skill at all. What you do need is the ability to push a trolley, to remember who takes what, and to listen. I can vouch for the last two being more useful than they sound. Forty-one years of keeping ledgers straight turns out to be surprisingly handy when you are trying to recall that one gentleman has milk and no sugar and the lady by the window will only have decaf after noon.

On a typical Thursday the unit sees fourteen to eighteen patients. Many of them come for the art group or the hand massage, and some come simply for company. Most go home afterwards. The room is noisy and rather jolly. People talk over each other, somebody is always telling a story they have told before, and the staff are running about with clipboards. I have seen it described as a sad place, and I suppose on some days it is. I will not pretend otherwise. Some weeks are hard, and there are days when a patient we have grown fond of is not there the following Thursday. When that happens, the staff look after us, and we talk about it among ourselves over the kettle. But most Thursdays it is not sad at all. It is mostly tea, gossip, and biscuits.

Speaking of biscuits: the bourbons always go first. We have learned to hide a packet for the late group, because otherwise there is nothing left by half past three, and there is a stern little lady who will let you know about it.

There is one of our regulars I must mention. Mr Hollis is a retired signalman, and he takes two sugars and insists on telling me about the 1953 floods every single week. The details shift a little each time. I have given up correcting the dates. It is one of the small pleasures of the afternoon.

My first week, I spilled an entire jug of milk over the trolley. I was mortified, and I was reaching for the cloth when a patient called Pat laughed so hard she had to be given a tissue. Afterwards she told me it was the best afternoon she had had in a month. I have never been quite sure whether that was about me or about the milk, but I have decided it was about the company, and I have stuck with that.

I would be lying if I said volunteering had changed my life in some dramatic way. What it did was give me a fixed reason to get out of the house. After I retired I had no regular reason to go anywhere most weeks, and for about eighteen months I drifted. Thursdays put an end to that. I now have a place I need to be, people who expect me, and a trolley that does not push itself.

So here is the practical part. If you are curious, come along to our volunteer open afternoon on Tuesday 24 November at 2pm in the Willow Room. There is tea and biscuits, and no obligation whatsoever. You can ask whatever you like, and nobody will be offended if you decide it is not for you. If you cannot make it on the day, ring Bridget on the volunteering line.

We would be very glad of at least two new people. You do not need to be clever, skilled, or brave. You need to be willing to push a trolley on a Thursday afternoon and to put up with a few stories about the floods.
